The axial-anomaly equation, which is fundamental to the physics of quarks and gluons, can't be fully understood in the framework of dimensional regularization. This renormalization scheme breaks some gauge and chiral symmetries, making it difficult to analyze the Euler-Heisenberg energy density, which is also dimensionally problematic. To overcome these issues, a gauge-invariant regularization scheme based on the higher-covariant derivative regularization is proposed. Using this new scheme, the dimensional regularization renormalization group equation for the flavor-singlet axial-vector current is re-derived, revealing a simpler renormalization structure. This re-derived equation can then be applied to the Euler-Heisenberg energy density to overcome the remaining dimensionful obstruction.

Capturing images with multiple cameras and fusing them to create a high-quality, colorful image is a common technique used in machine vision. However, the cameras used are typically from the same source, resulting in consistent colored depth maps. In contrast, using images from cameras with different color schemes to merge them into a colorful result is rare and presents significant challenges, mainly due to the differences in how color is displayed on various cameras. Our study investigates the effect of camera settings on machine vision and develops a novel approach called "color transfer" that transfers the visual characteristics of a high-quality, colorful image to a lower-quality, different colored image. The proposed method uses a multi-step process to transfer the color and tone from a reference image to a different colored image, maintaining accurate object shapes. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in improving machine vision performance.

Recent studies on the three-dimensional Ermakov system have been resolved, and we now apply the Noether theorem to the Lagrangian for further research on its general n-dimensional form. We identify 20 distinct symmetry elements and five conservation laws associated with the system, utilizing methods from differential algebra. Notably, the presence of a Killing tensor of rank two is also demonstrated.

Mobile public transportation is a crucial component in modern transit systems, with multiple agencies and routes requiring precise scheduling and reliable service.
A widely adopted solution, known as transit feed, has become a standard format, but it poses significant analysis and design challenges.
This study focuses on identifying the fundamental constraints that define feasible transit feed and demonstrates how these limits affect real-world data availability.
A detailed analysis of a specific transit network in Bangalore, India, revealed that nearly 90% of vehicles and 95% of routes are unavailable in the current feed format.
A decision tree model was developed to automatically detect missing passengers and schedule points, significantly improving data completeness.
The implementation of this system led to a substantial 40% increase in vehicles and schedules that could be represented in the feed format.
A specific decision rule was identified as the most influential factor in accurately identifying missing schedule points.
A recurrent neural network was then used to infer travel times between previously unrecorded schedule points, resulting in a substantial 80% increase in representable vehicles and schedule points.
This innovative approach enables a more comprehensive analysis of transit performance, particularly in complex urban environments.

This study explores the concept of intraclass variability in few-shot learning algorithms, examining its implications and effects. In contrast to existing metrics, such as the F1 score and recall rate, the proposed approach is uniquely capable of quantifying and comparing the intraclass variability of different methods, serving as a diverse benchmark for few-shot learning. In response to the identified variability concerns, the study then presents a novel approach, involving an intraclass prototype learning algorithm, which aims to optimize intra-class compactness and serve as a new baseline for few-shot learning. Experimental results validate the utility of intraclass variability analysis and demonstrate that the proposed approach, involving intraclass prototype prototype learning, outperforms existing methods.

We have derived a Goldstone theorem for a specific type of non-invertible chiral symmetry, with its underlying algebra based on a triangular lattice, in the context of a 3D spin system governed by a cubic Hamiltonian near a paramagnetic state. The system supports a collective variable functioning as a 'goldball' field, representing the non-invertible symmetry's Goldstone mode. When expanding this field under non-inertial transformations, we find that low-energy processes are constrained by a unique action equation featuring a topological anomaly. This result is verified through numerical and analytical large-N methods in the specific case of the $O(\text{Textr})$ goldball field's scattering amplitude.

A semi-transitive graph is a simple undirected graph that meets a specific condition. 
It has the property that for any three consecutive indices, not all edges between them are present. 
In this work, we define a graph as monochromatic if it has the same type of transitivity for all non-zero entries. 
A graph is quasisymmetric if it contains at least two monochromatic graphs. 
It was previously established that certain types of quasisymmetric split graphs can be colored with a specific set of colors. 
In this work, we demonstrate that split graphs lacking a specific set of patterns can also be colored with three colors.

A novel approach has been developed for detecting hadronic particle decays at the Large Hadron Collider's LHCb experiment, by training a multi-layered neural network on simulated data. The approach stands in contrast to traditional methods by directly analyzing raw particle data from tau decays, rather than using derived variables, and has been successfully tested on simulated tau decays at the LHC's HL-LHC phase. With a 95% tagging efficiency, this method achieves approximately 29% background rejection, outperforming existing solutions by a significant margin.

Future sky surveys from the LSST, Euclid, and the CMB-SPT and CMB-S4 experiments are expected to produce an immense amount of data. Leveraging machine learning will be crucial for processing these vast datasets to extract precise measurements of cosmic phenomena. Future surveys are expected to yield a significant increase in redshift survey precision. Accurate galaxy morphology classification is another key area where machine learning can make a substantial impact. This paper will delve into the use of Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNN) in tackling large-scale categorization tasks. Unlike traditional neural networks, BNNN has the ability to quantify uncertainty in their predictions, which is particularly beneficial for identifying and filtering out spurious data in future large-scale sky surveys. However, training BNNN on simulated datasets poses a significant challenge due to computational constraints, given the limited training data available. To overcome this hurdle, this study employs two breakthrough techniques: Stochastic BNNN training, which allows for training on minibatches, and a novel sampling-based training method, which allows training on multiple Monte Carlo samples. This paper will showcase its effectiveness by training stochastically-trained and sampling-based BNNN on simulated data.

Our research explores the character and implications of intermodal acoustic wave interactions driven by primary scattering processes within solid-core photonic lattice fibers. Through rigorous mathematical proofs and detailed numerical simulations, we examine intermodal linear resonance conditions and the behavior of forward Brillouin scattering nonlinearity in degenerate, partially index, and non-circularly symmetric photonic lattice fibers. To mitigate strong coupling of higher-order modes to acoustic waves, we observe a non-degenerate scattering phenomenon. Furthermore, we examine the effects of non-degenerate mode coupling on phase-matching, a phenomenon previously unaccounted for in single-mode fibers. This phenomenon poses significant challenges for intermodal nonlinear applications. Our findings also indicate that adjusting the core geometry to minimize coupling between specific higher-order modes may be necessary to achieve strong coupling with forward acoustic waves.

Inspired by a crucial result from Welch that laid the groundwork for understanding permutations with specific non-ascension properties, a permutation's connection to simple generators can be represented through Coxeter permutations, which have been similarly analyzed in relation to this theorem. A fundamental theorem's generalization for the B-type Coxeter group relies on extending key properties of permutations, specifically those with a certain non-ascension property, to signed permutations. A recent study established a direct and affine approach to this extended theorem.

Two related knapsack problem variants, the Set-Union Knapsack Problem and the Budgeted Maximum Coverage Problem, have been the subject of this research, which developed local search algorithms to tackle these combinatorial optimization challenges. These problems involve covering diverse demand with set resources within specific constraints, mirroring multiple demands in various practical applications. Given the NP-hard complexity of these problems and the limitations of LSA and LGreedy in solving them efficiently, this research developed new local search algorithms with superior performance. The algorithms utilize a novel swap strategy and symmetric block mapping to identify high-quality local optima, outperforming existing local search methods in solution quality and computational efficiency. The algorithms were further enhanced with an adaptive randomization technique and simulated annealing to escape local optima and discover better global solutions. The study's primary focus was on the theoretical analysis of LGreedy's local optimality under both set-weight and item-weight scenarios and the development of a hybrid local search algorithm, ALO, for Budgeted Maximum Coverage.

A substantial issue faced by online gaming companies, similar to retail businesses, is the problem of customer churn. In the context of online gaming, this challenge is even more pronounced, particularly when it comes to forecasting user behavior. Our research introduces an integrated framework for predicting churn among online gaming users, which is a significant concern for operators. This framework involves initial data processing, creating indicators, applying machine learning models, and evaluating the system's performance. By applying this comprehensive approach to a real-world online gaming dataset, consisting of over 180,000 users, our experiments demonstrate the high accuracy and efficiency of our model, which successfully captures dynamic user behavior.

We study the Ising Field Theory in an external magnetic field, specifically around a unique point called the Yang-Lee critical point, which is accessible only through complex magnetic field values. This unique point marks a phase transition of the theory, leading to the well-known minimal Conformal Field Theory $\mathcal{M}(3,4)$. We utilize this phase transition to derive the content of the theory when subjected to a real magnetic field. This content is characterized by an infinite set of operators, which we determine by leveraging a conformal solution developed by Corley, Ramgoolam and Trivedi. The operator spectrum is found to be consistent with recent numerical findings from lattice simulations.

We utilize a practical framework, Large-Momentum Effective Theory (Large-Momentum Theory, LAT1), to investigate transverse-momentum-dependent (TMD) parton distribution functions (PDFs). By decomposing TMD PDFs into a universal transverse-momentum-dependent (TMD) PDF and a process-dependent collinear-soft (CS) matrix element, which encodes the effects of ultralarge momentum via a Sudakov-Smirakov-Tamponi (SST) factor, this approach simplifies TMD PDF calculations in a power-counting consistent manner. We specifically analyze gluon PDFs and demonstrate how to perform perturbative calculations up to next-to-leading order (NLO) accuracy and one-loop order for one-loop SST factors. This provides a new strategy for achieving high-precision calculations for gluon TMD PDFs.

A novel method for the accurate calculation of the electron/positron-nucleus interaction in heavy-ion collisions, especially in the low transverse momentum range, is established based on the light-front electromagnetic current. This current remains valid across all momentum ranges, unlike conventional approximations applied in ordinary processes. Using this current, the total cross-section for electron/positron-nucleus interaction is precisely calculated, and compared with the results from the conventional lab-frame approach. Our findings suggest that in the low-p_T range, discrepancies of one to two orders of magnitude may occur between the cross-section calculations based on different methods. Furthermore, we have also calculated the cross-sections for electron/positron-nucleus interaction and identified that the cross-section calculated in the light-front approach is comparable to that of an equivalent muon-nucleus interaction.

To minimize cyclist fatalities and injuries, advanced alert systems are under development. These systems rely on sophisticated state estimation to track cyclists accurately, but current approaches lack crucial safety information. This research proposes a groundbreaking method to dynamically generate intuitive risk indicators based on real-time video. These risk descriptors, in the form of audio-visual symbols, convey immediate danger levels to the cyclist using a combination of audio and visual cues. By integrating context-aware technologies, the framework adapts to varying riding environments, ensuring accurate risk assessment. Key innovations include a sophisticated motion tracking system, real-time risk calculation, and an audio-visual communication system to enhance cycling safety. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this novel method in accurately tracking cyclists and generating meaningful risk indicators.

This paper proposes a reliable motion planning method for mobile robots with complex movements, focusing on navigating unstructured environments while considering the robot's control limitations, robot dynamics, and safety of the robot itself. A control barrier function based approach is developed to create a safe and robust path for autonomous mobile robots in a 3D environment. To achieve this, a self-healing control barrier function layer is integrated to ensure the safety of the robot during execution. By applying this method to a real-world scenario, we successfully tested it on a quadruped robot, demonstrating its effectiveness in navigating a 3D environment.

This study demonstrates that certain neural network models are more resistant to adversarial perturbations without requiring specialized techniques such as adversarial training, gradient masking, or curriculum learning. By comparing the performance of neural network models with various activation functions, we find that the parameter values within networks that are more vulnerable to perturbations are those which are clipped by the network's non-linear functions, thereby making them more susceptible to perturbation. Furthermore, the results suggest that the presence of network sparsity can also contribute to increased resilience against perturbation.

We approach singular limit theory to develop a new class of nonlocal deterministic traffic models based on a nonlocal distance function. These models are shown to converge to a generalized Hamilton-Jacobi equation as the nonlocal domain vanishes, with the proof of this result being novel in the context of traffic models. We also derive an entropy inequality for the singular limit and establish an L1 convergence rate between the limits and original models, with the convergence rate being proportional to the oscillation of the acceleration function. The models are capable of using a large class of acceleration functions and are able to avoid a weakness of a specific acceleration function, first demonstrated by Wang and Wang in a previous study. We show that the novel framework overcomes this limitation and can model realistic scenarios where cars may speed up or slow down unexpectedly. Furthermore, we prove that the singular limit satisfies an entropy inequality and that this property is utilized to prove the convergence of a time-discrete numerical scheme to the correct entropy-admissible solution of the limiting equation. The convergence of this scheme is also shown to be linear with respect to the time step size for a piecewise-constant acceleration function, with the convergence being linear in the specified condition.

A complex surface known as a dilation surface can be created by taking a finite-area hyperbolic surface and applying a continuous transformation, the rate of which is at most twice the original curvature. As a result, a new topological structure emerges, characterized by a detailed analysis of this surface's behavior under continuous transformation. This analysis yields a structured framework, characterized by a detailed graph, that accurately represents the dynamic behavior of a related function used in the analysis. Furthermore, a one-to-one correspondence is established between certain configurations of links formed from the surface's boundary and possible structures formed from these surfaces, allowing researchers to determine whether a specific structure can be formed from a given surface through continuous transformation.

This study presents a new approach for dimensionality reduction that relies on total
or higher-order dependency measures. We argue for the application of total correlation
instead of existing methods like k-means clustering, mutual information, and PCA. 
Total correlation offers several benefits, such as capturing dependency between dependent
variables, addressing real-world data limitations, and providing robustness in analysis.
We successfully applied total correlation to brain functional connectivity data and 
demonstrated through experiments that it yields superior results compared to other techniques, 
particularly in predicting subject age and gender. The proposed approach utilizes 
networks of brain regions and employs various feature extraction and machine learning algorithms 
for age and gender classification. The model's performance is evaluated using multiple total 
correlation-based features and statistical metrics like accuracy and F1-score.

The classical Segal-Bargmann transformation can be extended to a space defined by the Clifford algebra, where it is connected to the Taylor isomorphism in a specific way. Furthermore, this extension reveals a specific structure within a certain algebra related to holomorphic sections of a bundle that has a Hilbert space structure, thereby yielding an orthonormal basis in this space.

In this thesis, a Gaussian field's conditional process is derived through direct calculation. A key application involves a Brownian motion conditioned to follow a specific trajectory. The method developed here complements an existing algorithm by Fontes, Denker, and Denker in origin and objectives. Additionally, this research establishes a measurable function representing the conditional distribution, obtained from a Gaussian field restricted to a specific set of values. This result has far-reaching implications for studying the characteristics of Gaussian fields given specific observations.

A future military scenario is envisioned where an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) collaborates with a ground-based sensor network, linking them to facilitate data transfer. The sensor network is made up of multiple ground stations and is split into multiple segments to optimize its communication capabilities. The goal of the study is to understand how this linkage can be achieved and to develop an efficient method for configuring the ground-based sensor network to maximize end-to-end data transfer between the UAV and the network. The analysis takes into account the UAV's flight path and speed, as well as the sensor network's topology and the air-ground link quality. The simulation results show that a specific optimization approach can significantly increase the data transfer rate and highlight how varying flight speeds impact the efficiency of the proposed method.

The fifth generation of long-baseline neutrino observatories, led by DUNE, significantly revitalize the field of neutrino physics research. This deep underground experiment, utilizing a novel, 12.5-kiloton argon-based time projection chamber technology, coupled with a 1-kilometer-long off-axis neutrino source generated by a Fermilab-based 120 GeV proton accelerator, greatly enhances the understanding of fundamental neutrino properties, including CP violation and matter effects. This comprehensive review examines the anticipated scientific outcomes of the DUNE experiment within the coming decade.

The identification and enhancement of top quark jets play a crucial role in analyses aimed at studying high-$p_T$ quarks, a key aspect when examining new physics phenomena predicted by beyond the Standard Model scenarios. We utilized jet substructure properties captured in 2016 data taken at the CMS experiment with 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity and compiled them into generalized jet images at various resolutions using a generalized jet image (GJN) metric with $R=0.7$ and a more refined $r=0.2$. We then applied a supervised machine learning approach to distinguish these jets from QCD jets. The results showed that the XGBoost algorithm, trained with these jet images, outperformed traditional top-tagger algorithms in terms of both working point efficiency and signal-to-background ratios. We further analyzed the model's predictive capabilities using the Shapley additive explanation (SHAP) method, which allowed us to gain insights into the partonic origins of the jet images and their effectiveness in distinguishing top quark jets.

This work builds upon a paper from the proceedings of the 14th International Conference on Semantic Technologies for Knowledge and Data Systems (ICTASK2020), whose key insights are expanded upon here. The expansion includes a crucial refinement of Virtual Organizations relevant to process management, as well as a formal definition of this refinement. Furthermore, this research proposes and initially sketches out an approach for automatically inferring VOs refinements.

A key advantage of using policy optimization algorithms like TRPO and PPO, which are free from the need for model learning, is their sample efficiency. However, the non-stationary nature of the reward function, which varies with each sample, poses significant challenges to the convergence of these algorithms. A common technique used to mitigate non-stationarity in policy optimization is the experience replay buffer. Existing variance diminishing methods primarily focus on the mean-squared error of the data, which can result in a situation where the distribution of samples is heavily skewed towards high-reward samples. A new variance diminishing approach, which minimizes the difference between the actual and expected return of the samples by considering the current variance of the return distribution, is proposed. This approach is based on the concept of minimum variance unbiased estimator. A theoretical analysis demonstrates that our algorithm can effectively address the problem of non-stationarity in policy optimization and outperforms existing methods on the benchmark of Atari games.

Two recently introduced theoretical frameworks for analyzing interacting fermion systems are examined in this study. The first involves the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation, an extension of an existing method that facilitates analysis of interactions involving multiple channels. The second involves the superbosonization equation, an integral equation derived from superalgebra theory. For mutually commuting channels, it is demonstrated that these methods are fundamentally equivalent, an conclusion that is further supported by an derivation of the superbosonization equation from superalgebra theory involving the extended special unitary group U_n(osp) and its corresponding Lie superalgebra.

This research introduces a detailed approach to a recurrent neural network called MoDeRNN, specifically designed to handle spatiotemporal prediction tasks, like weather forecasting. The method involves a recurrent neural network that can accurately model the temporal dynamics of local pixel spaces through the application of 2D convolution. By training the network using pixel-wise recurrent connections, MoDeRNN can produce realistic predictions that accurately reflect temporal changes. Results demonstrate MoDeRNN's superior performance over traditional LSTM, particularly on the weather-related NextWind task, while maintaining efficient inference times and parameter usage.

In JavaScript, pointers do not exist, yet memory is still required, which is typically managed through references in modern frameworks. These references, however, frequently lead to intricate and error-prone patterns like Promises, Temporal Expressions, and React's Component tree, which are difficult to visualize due to their complexity. 

This paper introduces a new reference pattern called Josephines, a syntactically distinct type in the Rust language, which can be conveniently developed in the widely-used JavaScript language. The visual appearance of these patterns is significantly minimized, and their lifespan is clearly depicted within the code, allowing developers to easily comprehend program behavior. 

The paper also discusses how Josephines can be implemented within the Rust language, outlines the challenges encountered, and illustrates their utility in addressing a common problem - data propagation in the context of WebAssembly. The code examples used in this research are available in the Open Source project at github.com/marionebl/josephines.

This study investigates the relationship between neutrino properties and the likelihood of neutrinoless double-beta decay at high-energy colliders. Researchers have linked light and heavy neutrino masses to observable properties of neutrinos, excluding any influence from neutral, massive states in this relationship. Neutrinoless double-beta decay at colliders may be influenced by neutrino mixing angles and the neutrino mass influence factor related to charged-current processes. Researchers' analysis of double-beta decay experiments provides constraints on neutrino properties, which in turn impacts searches for this phenomenon at high-energy colliders.

Achieving reliable communication at a non-zero error rate while using the shortest possible code is a significant challenge in coding theory. Low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes, known for their capacity-approaching properties, are typically decoded using the belief propagation (BP) algorithm, which is an efficient iterative process. This research presents a novel decoding approach by incorporating the polar codes' channel splitting and freezing techniques into the BP-based decoding process. The method employs a subcode of the LDPC code to split the channel into multiple subchannels, assigns transmission probabilities to these subchannels, and freezes the messages on frozen variables to ensure the reliability of the most significant ones. The simulation results show that this polar-BP hybrid decoding method outperforms the existing methods by achieving better error correction performance at a short code length.

When images of a multi-component system are combined, the point spread functions of those components can be determined by combining the areas that are not influenced by any component, effectively isolating individual PSFs when the components are separated by a sufficient distance. This process can also be utilized to calculate the luminosity associated with each PSF.

To determine the fracture strength of crystals, we employed the tight-binding potential model in molecular dynamics simulations. By inverting our model, we found that fracture occurs when the largest interatomic distance reaches a specific fraction of the model's characteristic energy scale. Our simulations, which included simulations of fractures under tension and compression, showed that the interplay between Poisson's ratio and the model's model-dependent parameter significantly influences the stress required to cause fracture. Notably, our simulations revealed that Poisson's ratio greater than a critical threshold in model parameters results in the emergence of specific stress anomalies prior to fracture, which varied depending on whether the material underwent tensile or compressive deformation.

We establish a stochastic calculus for multivariate Brownian motion with exchangeable increments, derive its Itô formula, and apply it to derive an explicit SDE for joint SLEs motivated by the coupling of the Gaussian free field and $\mathrm{CLE}_{\kappa}$ for $\kappa\in(0,4)$.

In this study, we establish initial estimates for the solution of the Navier-St equations with data initially large in the $H^1$ and $H^2$ Sobolev spaces, expressed using the maximum metric $|\nabla P|+|\nabla u|$. Additionally, we address the issue of data initially large in the $H^2$ space and show an estimate in terms of the maximum metric for $H^2+$ data. We leverage a previously published method from [1, 2, 3, 4] by employing an iteration technique.

Over the next few decades, quantum computers are expected to challenge existing technology, making full-scale models difficult to operate. This creates a challenge in validating the outputs of quantum programs, which cannot be directly observed due to the probabilistic nature of quantum measurements. This study focuses on classical verification methods for quantum programs, aiming to determine if they can be executed in linear time, similar to classical programs. The analysis covers a range of quantum programming constructs, including data manipulation, quantum data manipulation, conditionals, and loops, finding that program verification is feasible in linear time if the program contains no recursive calls. Additionally, the study examines the use of quantum data in classical computations and the efficient use of quantum loops, and employs tree-based analysis methods to estimate the program's execution time and complexity.

A blockchain underpins a distributed ledger technology that is used in numerous applications, including secure identification of digital assets, data protection, and traceability in complex systems like food supply chains. By leveraging blockchain's inherent security, these applications can be reliably tracked. However, blockchains are hindered by their lack of direct access to external data, which limits their applicability. To overcome this limitation, we developed a customized blockchain framework that integrates with the Internet of Things, enabling external data access through trusted gateway devices. This framework is being tested by tracking the entire journey of an apple from its origin to the final consumer, with data exchange between the involved parties facilitated by the gateway and automatically executed by smart contracts.

Over the last decade, generative models that map latent space to image space have primarily focused on creating visually appealing images of natural scenes, but their potential to model living cells, particularly the intricate cytoskeletal networks, remains largely overlooked. We have thoroughly examined the effectiveness of various generative models in capturing the diverse forms of cells, including those undergoing division, and discovered substantial gaps in their performance. We have successfully utilized the CRN generative model to establish a correlation between the inherent properties of living cells and the underlying cytoskeletal components. Our research highlights the critical importance of generative models in understanding cellular processes such as division, proliferation, and the determination of cell identities.

Blind individuals often rely on screen readers to navigate documents formatted with HTML. However, many image-rich documents pose significant obstacles, limiting screen reader users' accessibility. In order to enhance screen reader usability, images within documents should be strategically replaced with captions, descriptions, or graphics substitutes. Our research aims to assess the amount of information provided by image-rich documents in relation to the overall content, with the goal of determining their screen reader navigability. A novel Document Navigability metric is introduced, accompanied by a graph-based method for evaluating the navigability of documents based on their image-to-text ratio. A comparison with existing image-rich document navigability assessments is also presented.

We propose XLPretraining, a pretraining task that unifies key features of ELMo and BERT models, surpassing BERT's pretraining on specific corpora with its attention to diverse contexts through context reconstruction. This development is guided by an innovative masking strategy and refined loss function. Experimentally, XLPretraining outperforms GPT and GPT-2 on multiple benchmarks. Moreover, a refined XLPretraining + ETL model demonstrates remarkable performance on numerous tasks, including long-text related ones, and achieves state-of-the-art results on several important benchmarks.

We've developed a statistical method to identify the influence of a star's activity on transmission spectra and applied it to transit data of planet HD 212856b observed at both low and high resolution. A significant feature was detected in the star's spectrum at 0.8 micrometers during the transit, indicating a concentrated area of activity on the planet. This feature was not present in earlier observations, suggesting a change in the activity pattern. High-resolution data provided valuable information by identifying the feature's radial velocity, which helped in understanding the star's movement. This helped in characterizing the feature further and estimating the size of the active region on the planet. This approach can be used to identify the influence of a star's activity in future exoplanet transmission spectroscopy data.

For any genus $g \ge 1$ Riemann surface $X$, along with $k_1$, $k_2$, $k_3$ integers satisfying $k_1 + 2k_2 + 3k_3 = 2g-2$, we demonstrate the existence of a unique Riemann surface metric with genuses $k_1$, $k_2$, $k_3$ singularities of orders $1$, $2$, $3$ respectively.

Research has confirmed that the centipede species Centruroides graeffei lives in desert environments near water sources, but its swimming abilities have not been previously studied. We investigated how this species navigates in shallow water, using high-speed video recordings and force measurements to understand its locomotion methods. We found that when swimming, this species uses the tip of its abdomen in the front and the legs in the back to maneuver through the water, similar to how the centripetal force in the fluid affects the movement of objects within the fluid. Our results show that when this species moves in the water, it experiences a form of drag that increases as a function of the speed of the movement, with an exponent of approximately 2.0. We also found that when this species moves in the water, it experiences a form of resistance that increases as a function of the speed of the movement, with an exponent of approximately 2.0. Our findings suggest that when this species moves in the water, it experiences a form of drag similar to that of the centripetal force in the fluid, with a similar pattern of movement, and suggests that when this species moves in the water, it experiences a form of resistance that increases as a function of the speed of the movement, with a similar pattern of movement.

A high-performance computing system is leveraged to run complex, large-scale simulations of atmospheric phenomena occurring after astronomical events like meteorites or asteroid impacts. These simulations involve multiple processes that take place across various spatial and temporal scales, which necessitate a highly optimized, parallel execution on a high-performance computing system to produce accurate results within a reasonable timeframe. Adjusting the level of detail in different areas of space and time is crucial for achieving this goal, and our research focuses on developing methods to dynamically adapt this level of detail across a high-performance computing system. We test and demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach using high-performance simulations of tsunami waves generated from an event like an asteroid impact, which is a phenomenon that is both physically and computationally challenging.

Recent observations of a specific population of highly luminous galaxies in the early universe, which cannot be explained by current models, have created significant interest. A thorough investigation of 12 highly luminous, low-surface-brightness galaxies identified through Herschel data, which we have conducted with the Near-Infrared Camera on the James Webb Space Telescope, has revealed important findings. The galaxy sample spans a range of redshifts, extending from 0.23 to 1.33, and spans the period of the cosmic star-formation peak. A notable characteristic of these galaxies is their low mass-to-luminosity ratio, which ranges from 0.002 to 0.009 solar masses per solar luminosity. A comparative analysis of the 12 galaxies with the Cosmic Evolution Experiment sample at the same redshifts has shown that the highly luminous galaxies exhibit a higher specific star-formation rate, lower mass-to-stellar ratio, and lower metal abundance. The high-resolution images from the NIRCam for a subset of the galaxy sample have allowed the detection of a high proportion of the luminosity in the form of dust, which was not detected in the Herschel observations. A detailed analysis of the 12 galaxies has revealed that the high dust content is primarily due to the presence of a diffuse, dust-rich halo rather than a merger event. The high optical depth of the halo has been demonstrated to significantly impact the detection of the far-infrared emission,

In four-dimensional gravity, as proposed by 't Hooft and Wolfram, certain additions can facilitate understanding of inherent issues. A seven-dimensional model incorporating similar adjustments is examined to address problems in four-dimensional theory. This analysis leads to the conclusion that a fundamental scale must be introduced, which in turn necessitates an inherent unit of length.

We investigate the problem of arranging a closed disk that is confined within a channel, alongside multiple weighted and sized semi-circular disks. We explore an iterative method that seeks to minimize the distance between the semi-circular and semi-circular-like disks. To substantiate the convergence of this algorithm, we prove the existence and uniqueness of a global minimizer for an associated objective function, considering two distinct cases where the weighted and sized semi-circular disks either all have the same or different sizes. Furthermore, we relate our result to a related problem involving a compact object instead of a blocked disk, and leverage our findings to solve a packing problem featuring two distinct sizes and weighted semi-circular disks in a channel.

To better understand and forecast imbalances in precipitation patterns,
identifying the distinct characteristics of individual El Nino-La Nina events
is crucial. Using the Nino3.4 time series from 1857-2019, 
two distinct flavors of these events were identified: 'shallow' and 'deep',
categorized according to significant thresholds. Analysis revealed that
rainfall patterns in events associated with 'deep' El Nino events are more
sensitive to its effects, particularly notable during 'deep' La Nina events,
characterized by more intense high-level precipitation. Conversely,
rainfall patterns in 'shallow' events show a significant difference in mean
precipitation, particularly notable during 'shallow' La Nina events.
Additionally, deep La Nina events show a significant difference in high-level
precipitation patterns, particularly notable during shallow La Nina events.
This study's findings provide valuable insights into the complex relationship
between El Nino-La Nina events and global precipitation patterns.

The dynamics of solid materials under stress can be categorized as either homogeneous or localized.  Homogeneous deformation is characterized by the uniform movement of particles, whereas localized deformation occurs when a material undergoes localized changes.  Research has shown that efficient light scattering techniques can be used to study and track the movement of particles within materials, thereby providing insights into their microscopic behavior.  These techniques can help to distinguish between different types of deformation and provide a deeper understanding of how materials respond to stress.  In particular, these methods can be used to investigate the behavior of soft and viscoelastic materials, thereby contributing to the broader field of non-affine growth research.

This research aims to develop a population model that considers the effects of age and environmental pollution on bipolar habitats. By formulating model equations based on the von Foerster model, we propose a single-species population model with age structure that reflects an organism's tendency to seek cooler environments. Moreover, we derive critical thresholds for the basic reproductive rates in both environments to determine population persistence and extinction, and introduce the concept of a bifurcation parameter to identify the transition between these states. Additionally, we obtain mathematical solutions for the population model and analyze the long-term behavior of single species with varying activities levels.

The researchers achieve decidable cut elimination in all hypersequent calculi belonging to the $S4$ and $S4G$ algebraic semantics classes, which are extensions of the standard classical logic. This achievement is a significant improvement upon earlier work and opens the door to future research on cut elimination in even broader classes of substructural logic, specifically those that allow the weakening and contraction rules. This research has practical applications in the design of hypersequent calculi for substructural logics that possess unusual properties.

Recent research has demonstrated the potential of using hyperbolic space for taxonomic representation learning due to the inherent hierarchical structure's compatibility. However, conventional representation learning techniques in hyperbolic space are restricted to processing static textual data and fail to capitalize on the dynamic nature of taxonomies, which incorporate novel categories over time as texts and subcategories evolve. To address this limitation, we introduce HyperExpan, a novel taxonomy learning framework that seamlessly integrates live text and existing categories in a hyperbolic space model. HyperExpan's capacity for expanding taxonomies surpasses HyperHIDE, the previous state-of-the-art taxonomy learning approach in experiments conducted on three taxonomy sets consisting of 575, 1,293, and 2,151 categories respectively.

Our research explores the impact of a static electric field on various intermolecular forces, revealing significant changes in their strengths and compositions. In contrast to earlier findings by other scientists, our experiments demonstrate that electric fields enhance the dispersion component of the forces while diminishing others, including the conventional quadrupole interaction in quadrupole-induced dipole forces. Additionally, our experiments show that electric fields can cause previously undetected forces to emerge, such as the magnetic dipole-induced dipole force. These findings highlight the crucial role electric fields play in determining the long-range intermolecular forces between molecules.

The fourth revolution in industry heavily relies on data and information technology advancements to boost productivity. A crucial component of this is Industry 4.0 scheduling, the effectiveness of which directly correlates with the overall production performance. However, traditional scheduling models struggle to account for non-deterministic factors common in modern manufacturing settings. In response, we propose a new method for resolving non-deterministic models by drawing from random data, offering a reliable solution with high probability. This approach is exemplified through its application to complex linear scheduling problems, incorporating real-world case studies.

This paper introduces an original concept of resilience for Cyber-Physical Systems grounded in Signal Temporal Logic. The framework is built on the restoration of invariance properties within a limited time frame after temporary disruptions occur. The time frame of recovery can vary based on the specific disturbance that has taken place. The framework's validity is established through a theoretical analysis and demonstrated in a case of a Magnetic Levitation System with potential failures. The approach also offers a tool for the design of resilient Cyber-Physical Systems within the framework of hybrid invariance-based control. The necessary design requirements for such systems are clearly outlined and a specific CPS is designeD to satisfy these requirements. The resilience of the designed CPS is subsequently verified and shown through comparative simulations against a non-resilient CPS counterpart.

A new approach to detecting dark matter signals from isospin-violating interactions involves analyzing the displacement of large masses. Although seismological networks are not designed for this purpose, they offer a large existing infrastructure that can be repurposed to search for such signals. This proposal outlines the potential to upgrade existing networks for this purpose, develops a simulation to calculate expected signal patterns, and explores various analysis techniques to distinguish signals from noise. Furthermore, the proposal recommends searching for horizontal displacements in addition to vertical ones to enhance detection capabilities.

This paper introduces a new category of quantitative information flow by employing category theory and the theory of monadic signatures. Specifically, we extend the theory of hidden Markov models (HMMs) to the theory of abstract hidden markov models (AHMMs). Our approach provides a comprehensive, category-theoretic description of how to compose systems that leak quantitative information. In the context of real-world programming, our theory facilitates the creation of libraries for quantitative information flow. Additionally, our theory builds upon the existing work of hiding processes by Abrial et al., allowing for a comparable category-theoretic description of hiding. Crucially, we extend the ability to hide interactive processes with the capability of representing side effects quantitatively.

Nonlocal-in-space and nonlocal-in-time phenomena are widely observed across diverse systems, yet the connection between them remains unexplored. A statistical analysis examines the relationship between the spatio-temporal nonlocality of turbulent flows and the persistence of coherent structures in isolated turbulent systems over a wide range of Reynolds numbers. Novel techniques for spatial and temporal nonlocal characterization are introduced to quantify the level of nonlocality in various scales. By applying a nonlocal-in-space and nonlocal-in-time measure to turbulent flows, it is discovered that certain structures remain isolated over extended periods of time due to their overall nonlocal-in-space and nonlocal-in-time nature. Furthermore, it is observed that in fully developed turbulent flows, isolated structures maintain their overall nonlocal-in-time properties despite being locally nested across different turbulent scales. It is hypothesized that this inherent nonlocal-in-time characteristic is a direct consequence of the nonlocal-in-space nonlocal-in-time properties. These findings provide a new perspective on nonlocal-in-time behavior in isolated turbulent structures and offer a new way to investigate the long-term behavior of turbulent coherent structures.

The accuracy of standard model predictions for high-precision measurements at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) is compromised by QCD corrections, necessitating precise calculations up to next-to-next-to-leading order (NNLO) and beyond. This paper introduces a novel approach to accurately resolve renormalization and factorization scales at NNLO and higher orders in perturbation theory an expansion. This method, dubbed Flexible Scattering Phenomenology (FSP), employs a probabilistic scale setting algorithm that minimizes scale uncertainty and scale-dependent loop corrections, respectively. FSP has been applied to precise DY cross-section and differential distributions at NNLO in QCD. Results indicate a substantial reduction in scale variations, on par with current state-of-the-art electroweak corrections. Furthermore, FSP has been utilized at NNLO for distinct differential distributions, significantly scale-insensitive.

This work examines how the Casimir effect influences the state of a single particle's blackbody, specifically when subjected to transverse and specific boundary conditions. A single particle in a box is considered, which serves as a model for an atom or nanoparticle. The calculation of energy levels follows the method introduced by Pathria, with adjustments for the impact of electromagnetic fields. The adjustments are made to both the particle's kinetic and thermal energy levels. The impact of the Casimir effect and boundary conditions on the particle's thermodynamic behavior is then analyzed. Theoretical transverse and parallel limits are considered, with the parallel condition modeled as a metal plate separated by a small distance. A solution to the Schrödinger equation follows the method proposed by Schrodinger for a particle confined between two infinite potential walls. The calculation of partition and thermodynamic function logarithms are performed using standard statistical mechanics principles. The work demonstrates that the Casimir effect significantly impacts blackbody thermodynamics, with boundary conditions playing a significant role in this influence. The impact on thermal excitation energy levels and specific heat capacity has been specifically analyzed. The work also considers the impact of the Casimir effect on thermal excitation energy levels and the thermodynamic properties of blackbody radiation. The impact of the Casimir effect on thermal excitation energy levels and the thermodynamic properties of blackbody radiation. The impact of the Casimir effect on thermal excitation energy levels and the thermodynamic properties of blackbody radiation.

This work focuses on protecting long term location tracks under a conditional prior model for an adversary's belief about a user's track history. We've developed two key results for establishing this protection: Firstly, we've derived a conditional version of the maximum differential privacy (MDP) and the zero-order differential privacy (ZODP) concepts along with their relationship to track privacy. Secondly, we've introduced two novel metrics called conditional sensitivity and random walk index (RWI) that serve as bounds for conditional differential privacy and track privacy respectively. Both MDP and ZODP bounds can effectively be applied to real-world datasets for both indoor and outdoor environments to ensure protected long term location tracks.

The integration of the Normal Distribution Transform (NDT) representation and the attention mechanism has led to the creation of NDT-Transformer, a 3D point cloud localization framework. NDT-Transformer, which is inspired by the well-established Transformer in the context of Pose Estimation from 3D Point Clouds (PEPC), overcomes the limitations of the Transformer's inapplicability to 3D point cloud data. NDT-Transformer, which is modular and parameterized, consists of two sub-modules: the NDT-Encoder and the NDT-Decoder. The NDT-Encoder, which consists of an NDT model and a point descriptor learning module, creates global and pairwise relationships between reference and target point clouds. The NDT-Decoder, which uses the attention mechanism, estimates the optimal transformation between these point clouds. Comprehensive evaluations on the KITTI and HoloMap datasets have shown that NDT-Transformer achieves superior performance in terms of accuracy and efficiency, as well as robustness.

Research has demonstrated that functional connectivity between brain regions can be used to differentiate between individuals, however, the reproducibility of this metric remains poorly understood. This study aimed to assess the reliability and predictive accuracy of functional connectivity patterns in multiple sites. By analyzing 1,274 scans from 388 participants across 1,216 brain regions, this study calculated the inter-rater reliability of functional connectivity between pairs of regions. The findings revealed significant variation in functional connectivity measures, ranging from nearly perfect to nearly zero correlation, across all brain region pairs. Furthermore, this study found that, in general, as the number of sampled scans increased, functional connectivity measurements became more accurate, across all site combinations. By averaging multiple scans per subject, this study demonstrated that, compared to a single scan, functional connectivity could better distinguish between individuals, however, this improvement became less noticeable as the number of sampled scans increased. This improvement was accompanied by substantial inter-site variability in prediction accuracy. This study also revealed that, as the number of sampled scans increased, functional connectivity-based predictions of a specific brain region's location in another, unshared dataset, became significantly more accurate, across all site combinations. The findings highlight significant inter-site variability in functional connectivity measurements and suggest that, to enhance functional MRI-based predictions, it is crucial to collect and analyze a large number of scans from each individual.

We investigate the minimum number of energy-exchange operations required for a notification-based network identification system, focusing on the simplest network consisting of isolated nodes that can only communicate when in close proximity and only perform two actions: wake up to listen, and sleep to conserve energy. Each notification is transmitted as a brief signal, and we explore a basic identification protocol using repeated transmissions of the same signal, demonstrating its inefficiency, particularly in the case of linear networks where it requires at least $O(n^2)$ operations, compared to $n$ nodes. In contrast, we introduce a more efficient randomised approach achieving $O(n^{1.5})$ operations on average, significantly reducing energy consumption. Nonetheless, employing deterministic methods results in significantly higher lower bounds of $n^3$ operations on paths and grids, highlighting the value of randomness in such networks.

The concept of Code-Mixed Linguistics has gained significant attention in the research community, with researchers exploring its complexity and ambiguity to develop novel approaches for Natural Language Processing (NLP). This paper introduces a pioneering technique that utilizes switching points to parse Code-Mixed languages into distinct regions: lexical and grammatical. By creating a code-based embedding model for each segment, we develop a Positional Encoding (PE) system to represent the structure of the language at a syntactic level. Our experiments on two code-switched Hindi datasets - the Long-form generation task (WMT 2021) and Machine Translation (IWLST 2020) - show that our Relative PE model outperforms other models by 4.5% and 3.4% in terms of performance. Furthermore, the experimental results validate the hypothesis that PE can be used to represent code-switched sentences more effectively, with switching point detection models achieving an F1 score of 80.3% and 84.3%.

Using a combination of first-principles calculations and Landau superfluid theory, the electronic and superconducting properties of H$_3$S under high pressure were studied in detail. The hybrid functional was employed to obtain accurate band structures and determine the presence of a van Hove singularity near the Fermi level, significantly enhancing the superconducting properties. The hybrid functional's prediction of H$_3$S's critical temperatures ($T_c$) is in good agreement with experimental results. The $A_{1g}$ phonon mode, responsible for $T_c$, is significantly affected by electron-phonon coupling near the singularity, which also gives rise to a notable isotope effect, particularly at higher pressures where the $T_c$ approaches its experimental upper limit. The predicted $T_c$ values and corresponding isotope effects for H$_3$S at various isotopes and pressures are presented in tables.

This paper introduces an innovative approach to motion planning for mobile robots moving within dynamic environments. Our new method generates constrained spatial areas to facilitate planning within environments that change over time. Our observation is that motion planning becomes more efficient when incorporating constraints derived from the environment's dynamics. Our framework comprises two key components: a conformational space, representing all possible robot motions, and a dynamic space, representing all possible environments. Our goal is to derive a constrained spatial area, where intersections between the conformational space and the constrained area form a space called the motion space, reflecting feasible robot motions. The proposed approach transforms the motion planning motion space into the space of motion plans, representing sequences of states that a robot follows. A demonstration of our approach is given through a simple scenario and implemented in the planning library MoveIt! with additional examples of more complex situations.

Visual localisation is a critical component of many robotic systems that relies heavily on accurately determining a camera's position in three-dimensional space. The efficiency and accuracy of visual localisation methods are typically hindered by map learning processes. We have developed an efficient method for rapidly relocalising cameras using learned, robust descriptors and a simplified representation based on surfels, which enables the efficient update of this representation in real-time on mid-range hardware. The reliability of our method is further enhanced through the use of pose covariances, which helps to distinguish between successful and unsuccessful relocalisation attempts. The accuracy and efficiency of our method have been demonstrated through extensive testing, achieving an average error rate comparable to state-of-the-art methods while significantly reducing the computational cost associated with map learning and track maintenance.

In Multi-Input Multi-Output systems, the combined approach of determining mobile device placements and optimizing precoding techniques can significantly enhance performance compared to implementing them separately. Research has shown that stochastic geometry can be utilized to simultaneously tackle these issues through the application of a specific type of regularization known as group LASSO. In a specific scenario where devices have only two antennas, it's possible to draw a direct equivalence between the iterative process of solving the group LASSO and a specific type of mathematical function. Furthermore, it's also been found that the most effective strategy in this situation is to use multiple beams for each transmitter, with its direction determined by the transmitter with the strongest channel for that antenna. Furthermore, with more advanced scenarios involving higher numbers of antennas, the equivalent strategy is to use beam directions determined by the top antennas with the strongest channel. Moreover, the stochiometric method of solving the group LASSO is able to be utilized to harness the full potential of these advanced scenarios. In a specific two-device scenario involving multiple antennas, the results of the different methods have been compared and evaluated, with a specific method being able to significantly outperform another method in terms of overall performance.

We demonstrate that the rational function semifield of a tropical curve, denoted as $\mathcal{TF}(\Gamma)$, contains a subsemifield, $\mathcal{S}(\Gamma)$ with a finite number of generators over the tropical semifield $\mathbb{T}=\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ with operations $\max$ and $+\$. The subsemifield $\mathcal{S}(\Gamma)$ is generated by a specific set, denoted as $\mathcal{S}(\Gamma)_{fin}$, and lies within the rational function semifield. To find this set of generators, we establish the tropical curve analogue of the "weak Nullstellensatz" by proving the "tropical curve Jacobson property." Furthermore, given the "Nullstellensatz" of a tropical curve, denoted as $\mathcal{Z}$, and its corresponding tropical polyhedron, denoted as $\mathcal{P}$, we demonstrate the inclusion of $\mathcal{S}(\Gamma)_{fin}$ in the rational function semifield of the corresponding tropical polyhedron $\mathcal{P}$. Additionally, given the rational function semifield of a tropical polyhedron, $\mathcal{TF}(\mathcal{P})$, we establish the finite production of the latter over the tropical semifield $\mathbb{T}=\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$.

In binary classification, the quality of predictors can be quantified by their excess risk, a more sensitive measure than the probability of incorrect prediction.  We compare two classifiers by examining the difference in their excess risks, which is more closely related and likely to converge faster with sample size.  We focus on the difference in excess risks converging to zero uniformly over all possible distributions within a certain probability class.  Unlike existing work, we show that the difference in excess risks can converge uniformly for distributions satisfying only certain marginal probability conditions.  Moreover, we establish not only the rate of convergence but also provide a specific upper bound on the difference in excess risks for each distribution within the class.

A vital component in the proof that the 2/5-Thurston norm ball is convex in a specific torus bundle over a five-punctured sphere is demonstrating that a particular loop can form a proper embedding after performing a single crossing change. This development has led to a more general theory involving a nontrivial Vassiliev invariant of order three and a novel relation called the 'box relation.' Furthermore, by examining the Vassiliev invariant and its connection to the Lie algebra, one can derive a comprehensive formula for counting branched covers that nullify this invariant.

Our study focuses on the role of spin fluctuations in nematicity within LiFeAs, using a comprehensive theoretical analysis, including both spin fluctuation calculations and optical conductivity measurements. Notably, our results show spin fluctuations have a minimal impact on nematicity in LiFeAs, unlike how they contribute significantly to it in other Fe-based superconductors. This finding, however, contrasts with the strong spin fluctuations observed in LiFeAs, raising the possibility that spin fluctuations may not directly cause spin-fluctuation-mediated nematicity in Fe-based superconductors.

We investigate two-variant two-Higgs-doublet models globally with renormalization group evolution up to the Planck scale and vacuum stability considerations, specifically models A2b, where a down-type particle's Yukawa coupling flips its sign in comparison to an up particle, and A2c, where a lepton charge difference reverses this relationship. Our research aligns these models' projections with the results of Higgs coupling and scalar production measurements from future colliders such as the FCC, ILC, CLIC, and LHCp, as well as dark matter constraints from the XENONnT direct detection experiment.

We introduce an advanced method of neuroevolutionary learning designed to tackle the complex challenge of self-assembly. This strategy, referred to as neuroevolutionary learning, involves agents or particles being assigned a goal to reach a target area of the space. To address the issue of efficiently searching vast configuration spaces, we introduce a novel neuroevolutionary algorithm that can identify novel strategies for self-assembly. By demonstrating the method's effectiveness, we show that it surpasses traditional approaches, such as reinforcement learning, when dealing with the significant challenges of non-rewarding intermediate stages and target identification. As an initial step, our results highlight the influence of the method's parameters on its performance and configuration space search capabilities. Furthermore, we propose an extension of the method allowing for cooperative problem-solving among multiple agents to address the issue of collective self-assembly problems.

Our research involves the study of anomaly and phase anomalies as well as their detection through topological indices in the context of chiral gauge theories. The analysis of the anomaly of the $SU(N)$ gauge theory with $n_f$ massless chiral fermions in the fundamental representation reveals an anomaly present when $n_f \le N-2$, whereas it is absent for $N+2 \ge n_f \ge N$, with phases appearing for $4N \ge n_f \ge N + 2$. Additionally, the presence of an anomaly in the $U(N)$ gauge theory with $n_f$ massless chiral fermions in the fundamental representation is established for $n_f \le N-2$, whereas it is absent for $N + 2 \ge n_f \ge N$, with phases appearing for $4N \ge n_f \ge N + 2$.

This study examines the properties of the three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations in various Besov spaces, and we demonstrate that if a specific condition is met then the equation in a particular space is not well-defined. We then look at the solvability of the equation when initial data within certain ranges, and show that when initial data within a larger range, the equation is not well-defined. We utilize multiple approaches in our investigation, including one that does not depend on small initial data, and we hope that this work will shed light on the properties of the equation.

We are investigating the phenomenon of thermal squeezing in magnons within specific types of magnetic materials when exposed to a GIG mode drive. Through rigorous theoretical analysis through second and fourth order perturbation techniques, we have found that the frequency of GIG mode has a non-linear shift in frequency due to thermal interactions. The thermal amplitude of magnons is influenced by both the temperature and interaction strength of these magnons, and its effect leads to nonlinearity in frequency. Notably, thermal interactions have a non-local character. A particular type of interaction known as the vertex type results in the modulation of magnon frequency. Additionally, we have identified the conditions necessary for achieving thermal squeezing with GIG mode synchronization. The findings presented in this study hold significant promise for developing a high-precision magnon engine.

Mitsuru Oki and Masaya Sasaki introduced two modifications to Oki-Sasaki's Loidreau's system, which has been proven to be vulnerable to a known-plaintext attack. We successfully developed an efficient algorithm to recover the underlying secret code with high probability in the Oki-Sasaki Loidreau's system under the known-plaintext attack, also making the secret code with a high probability accessible for both systems under a generic known-plaintext attack.

Language pre-trained models like Dict-BERT, which rely on self-attention and word embeddings, can be improved by addressing their limitations in handling word relationships and out-of-vocabulary words. A thesaurus can provide a more comprehensive understanding of word connections, enabling a more accurate assessment of similarities between words. By incorporating the thesaurus into these models, we can substitute word embeddings with thesaurus-enabled layers, combining the benefits of self-attention and word relationships. This enhancement leads to better model performance, as evidenced by our experiments incorporating the thesaurus into the Word-BERT model, yielding a +1.1% improvement in the F1 score on the WikiText dataset. Additionally, our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of incorporating the thesaurus into the dict-bi-GRU model, yielding a +0.6% improvement in the F1 score on the Coarse-Grained ICD dataset.

We analyze the asymptotic behavior of the distribution of minimal spanning subgraphs of a given complex and the persistence diagrams of such subgraphs under various assumptions about vertex space measurements. We also explore the theoretical mass properties of these graphs in relation to complex variables, considering three different distribution scenarios for these measurements at a vertex space point.

Federated learning is a groundbreaking technique for training machine learning models while preserving data security and governance.
Its main implementation, horizontal federated learning, involves keeping client data intact and aggregating model gradients.
This method has been found to successfully resist various privacy attacks.
However, its data security and governance benefits are not entirely assured.
In fact, they can be compromised when the central server has access to model architecture, training parameters, or other relevant information.
To address this issue, we developed the vertical federated learning VAMP, a novel tool to assess data privacy risks in this context.
This tool allows researchers to simulate data leakage attacks without requiring actual client data, making it a versatile solution for multiple use cases.
Using VAMP, we investigated memory inference and architeccture inference attacks and discovered surprising results.
This study demonstrates the significance of accounting for model architecture when evaluating data privacy risks in this context.
The developed VAMP tool is available for download at https://github.com/iamchenqi/VAMP-FL.

We predict the decay rate of the $B$-meson into a proton and an hypothetical dark antibaryon $d\bar{p}$, as well as relevant form factors, by utilizing the light-cone series expansion method. Our analysis reveals that first-order contributions to the relevant form factors are directly proportional to the $B$-meson's $\Lambda$ parameter and can be substantially modified by higher-order effects. Additionally, the decay rate is found to be closely linked to the magnetic moment of the dark antibaryon.

The ongoing integration of city infrastructure with sophisticated technologies such as public transport, energy systems, and water supply creates new opportunities and vulnerabilities. As these systems become smarter, they also become targets for malicious attacks on cyber and physical infrastructure, which can be triggered by a single actor or a coordinated campaign. To address this issue, we introduce a groundbreaking framework that integrates socio-cyber-physical layers, considering the dynamic interplay between these domains. Within this framework, we simulate a city defense strategy game, in which players must balance resource allocation and manage risks to protect their city from potential threats. Our game's resource management component reveals how efficiently cities can allocate resources, while its game-theoretic model reveals the strategic behavior of defenders and attackers. Our study reveals that investing in defensive measures not only deters potential attacks but also optimizes resource usage, and that a game-theoretic approach yields more accurate and valuable insights than traditional simulation methods.
